findings.description: The RDS instance sets storage_encrypted = false, so the database volume and snapshots store data in plaintext with no KMS customer-managed key.
publicly_accessible = true gives the RDS instance a public IP/endpoint, exposing the MySQL service to the internet rather than keeping it in a private subnet layer.
The master username is the default 'admin', a predictable account name that aids credential guessing/brute-force against the publicly reachable database.

The master password is supplied through var.password, a plain Terraform variable that is stored unencrypted in state and is likely committed/passed in plain text rather than sourced from Secrets Manager.

The EC2 user_data embeds the database username and password (var.password) in plaintext; user data is readable by anyone with ec2:DescribeInstances or via the instance metadata service, exposing the DB credentials.

No metadata_options block is defined, so IMDSv1 remains enabled; an SSRF in the PHP application would allow unauthenticated retrieval of the instance role credentials, which carry s3:*, ec2:*, rds:* permissions.
No root_block_device/ebs encryption is configured, so the instance's volumes — which hold the dbinfo.inc file containing DB credentials — are unencrypted at rest.
The instance is placed in a subnet and exposes a public DNS name (see output), serving an unencrypted HTTP application with no TLS, so credentials and form data transit in cleartext.

The instance role policy grants s3:*, ec2:*, and rds:* on Resource "*", which is effectively administrative over those services and allows privilege escalation and data access far beyond the app's needs.
The database security group permits all outbound traffic on all protocols to 0.0.0.0/0, providing a data exfiltration and command-and-control channel.
The MySQL parameter group does not set require_secure_transport = 1, so the database accepts unencrypted client connections; the PHP client also connects without TLS.
The database endpoint is exported as a non-sensitive Terraform output alongside a publicly accessible database, making the target readily discoverable to anyone with state or output access.
